system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 4 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2131-07-12 18:57:00 to 2131-07-16 14:00:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension, and multiple abdominal surgeries was admitted for acute epigastric pain, nausea, and bilious vomiting lasting four days, along with a report of black stool. Initial evaluation revealed leukocytosis and guaiac-positive stool, but normal pancreatic enzymes and no evidence of bowel obstruction or pulmonary embolism on CT imaging. His acute kidney injury, likely pre-renal from dehydration, resolved with IV fluids. Pain improved with supportive care, and he was advanced to a regular diet. New right-sided numbness and weakness were noted but CT head showed no acute pathology. He was discharged home with improved symptoms, instructions to restart diabetes medications with adequate intake, and follow-up with his primary care provider.
problems: Nonspecific abnormal findings in stool contents
Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, uncontrolled
Bipolar I disorder, most recent episode (or current) unspecified
Other musculoskeletal symptoms referable to limbs
Personal history of venous thrombosis and embolism

radiology_notes.text:
CHEST, TWO VIEWS:  ___

HISTORY:  ___ male with abdominal pain and vomiting.  Question free
air or pneumomediastinum.

FINDINGS:  AP and lateral views of the chest are compared to previous exam
from ___.  The lungs remain clear.  There is no effusion or
pneumothorax.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette appears normal.  No free air is
seen below the diaphragm.

IMPRESSION:  No acute cardiopulmonary process.

INDICATION:  Abdominal pain in patient with chronic pancreatitis and history
of Puestow procedure.

COMPARISON:  CT abdomen from ___ and ___.

TECHNIQUE:  MDCT-acquired axial images from the lung bases through the pubic
symphysis were obtained after administration of enteric contrast.  Due to a
technical error, the patient only received a pre-bolus of intravenous contrast
which was in the collecting system by the time of the scan.  Multiplanar
reformation performed to generate coronal and sagittal image series.

FINDINGS:  There is minimal dependent atelectasis within the lungs, and the
lower chest is otherwise unremarkable.

No focal liver abnormalities are seen. Diffuse hypodensity within the liver
suggests fatty infiltration. The patient is status post cholecystectomy and
Puestow procedure.  The pancreaticojejunostomy and jejunojejunostomy appear
intact and unchanged.  There are scattered coarse calcifications throughout
the pancreas with pancreatic atrophy consistent with chronic pancreatitis. 
There is no fluid collection or peripancreatic fat stranding to suggest acute
inflammation.  Main pancreatic duct does not appear enlarged. Common bile duct
measures up to 8-mm, but this is unchanged. The spleen, adrenal glands, and
kidneys are unremarkable.  The stomach, duodenum, and intra-abdominal loops of
small and large bowel are without focal wall thickening, dilation, or mass. 
There is no mesenteric or retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy.  The abdominal
aorta is not enlarged and contains scattered atherosclerotic calcifications. 
There is no intra-abdominal free fluid or air.  Patient is status post a prior
mesh repair of ventral hernia.  There is no residual herniation.  The bladder,
prostate, and seminal vesicles are normal.  The rectum and sigmoid appear
normal.  There is no pelvic free fluid or mass.  There is no pelvic or
inguinal lymphadenopathy.  There are no focal osseous lesions concerning for
malignancy.

IMPRESSION:  
1.  No acute intra-abdominal process to explain patient's symptoms.  
2.  Stable findings of chronic pancreatitis with no evidence of peripancreatic
fluid collection or acute inflammatory changes.  
3.  Stable post-operative changes from cholecystectomy, ventral hernia repair
and Puestow procedure.
4.  Hepatic steatosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, I’ve had this sharp pain in my lower left side for about four days now. It’s constant and goes into my back. It’s worse than my usual pancreatitis pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And does the pain get better or worse with eating or moving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, it doesn’t seem to change with food or bowel movements. I’ve also been nauseous and threw up a few times. I haven’t been able to keep anything down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Any fever, chills, or weight loss?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I felt like I had a fever, but I didn’t check. I did lose about 20 pounds recently, but I’m not sure why.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ve reviewed your CT scan from today. It shows stable chronic pancreatitis—no new inflammation or blockages. Your liver has some fat, but nothing urgent.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not acute pancreatitis? I was worried it might be worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, your lipase is normal, and the CT doesn’t show signs of acute inflammation. This looks like a flare of your chronic condition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had these flares before. But this one’s really painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to keep you NPO—nothing by mouth—for now to let your pancreas rest. You’ll get fluids through your IV and pain meds to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: How long will I be NPO?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll reassess tomorrow. Once your pain improves and nausea is controlled, we’ll start with clear liquids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. What about my diabetes? I usually take pills, but I haven’t eaten.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. We’ve started you on a sliding scale insulin to manage your blood sugar while you’re not eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thanks. And my pain meds—I usually need something strong.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve started a Dilaudid PCA pump so you can control your pain safely. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had a celiac plexus block a while back. Did that help? I don’t remember much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you had one recently. It can help, but since your pain is flaring again, we’re focusing on medication and rest for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. How’s your pain today?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Still there, but the IV meds are helping. I haven’t vomited since yesterday.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Your labs are improving. We’re going to try advancing your diet to clear liquids today if you’re up for it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, but I’m nervous. Last time I ate too soon, I threw up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll go slow—start with ice chips and broth. If you tolerate it, we’ll build up. We’re also continuing your pancreatic enzymes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Pancreaze, right? I take that with meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. We’ll restart that when you’re on solid food. Also, your EGD showed Grade C esophagitis—reflux is likely contributing to your nausea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had heartburn for years. I’m on omeprazole and Zantac.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep the omeprazole twice daily, but we’re stopping Zantac. It’s not needed with the higher omeprazole dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, fine by me. Any other changes?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted the chronic pain team. Given your history, they don’t recommend more procedures. They suggest discussing Suboxone for pain with your PCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Suboxone? For pain? I thought that was for addiction.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can help with chronic pain too, especially in patients with a history like yours. It’s safer than long-term opioids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Huh. I’ll ask my doctor about it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. You’ve been on a soft diet since yesterday and no vomiting. Pain is much better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yeah, it’s way better. I’m actually hungry.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re going to switch you to oral pain meds—Dilaudid tablets as needed. We’ll watch how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I get a prescription when I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, a one-week supply. But no refills. We want you to follow up with your PCP to discuss long-term pain management.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. What about constipation? The pain meds always mess me up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re adding Miralax and senna—take them as needed to stay regular.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my trazodone—I take 300 mg at night.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re reducing that to 100 mg as needed. Higher doses can cause side effects, especially with your history.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll try it. I just need to sleep.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs are stable. You’ve been tolerating a full diet, and your abdomen is much less tender. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What do I need to do when I get home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Continue all your regular meds except Zantac. Take Dilaudid only as needed for pain, and use Miralax and senna if you’re constipated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my follow-up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: See your PCP within a week. They’ll review your pain plan and the IgG test we ordered to check for autoimmune pancreatitis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I have an appointment next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. You look much better—pain is mild, you’re eating well, and your labs improved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks, doc. I feel a lot better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Remember: take the Dilaudid only as needed, stay on your enzymes with meals, and follow up with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll ask about that Suboxone option.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good idea. Also, call if the pain worsens or you can’t keep food down. Otherwise, take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do. Thanks again.

summary.summary_paragraph: A 50-year-old male with a history of chronic pancreatitis, GERD, and prior Puestow procedure was admitted for a four-day history of worsening left lower quadrant abdominal pain radiating to the back, nausea, and vomiting, with inability to tolerate oral intake. Initial CT showed stable chronic pancreatitis without acute findings, and labs supported a non-acute etiology. He was managed with NPO status, IV fluids, and a Dilaudid PCA for pain control. His symptoms improved over several days, allowing advancement to a full diet and transition to oral pain medication. GERD was addressed with continuation of omeprazole and discontinuation of ranitidine following EGD-confirmed Grade C esophagitis. Diarrhea resolved during admission. He was discharged home with a one-week supply of oral Dilaudid, instructions to use Miralax and senna for constipation, and a plan to follow up with his primary care provider for long-term pain management, including consideration of Suboxone. An IgG subclass test was ordered to evaluate for autoimmune pancreatitis.
